messages.subject: Area transition rates
messages.body_plain:
Hi BioGeo Group,

Does anyone know a way quantify the number of transitions into/out of each area? I want to test the hypothesis that an environmental barrier between two areas precludes recolonization of ancestral areas as a result of specialization. Once a lineage specializes enough to colonize area C it is less likely/able to diverge back into B or A.

Any insight on how to test this or general advice on analyzing transition dynamics from BioGeoBEARs output would be greatly appreciated.

Best,
Chauncey

messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] Area transition rates
messages.body_plain:
Hi! The "easiest" way to do this would be Biogeographical Stochastic Mapping -- google it for the script etc. You would get a sample of histories, each one as a table of events, and then go through those tables and count up the dispersal events and their directionality etc.  You could also do this under several different models and compare them.

The hard part is understanding the table structure and figuring out how to use R to e.g. count events in a table. This isn't "hard", but there is no tutorial written on it, it mostly depends on general R skills, so if you are willing to invest some time you can make it work.

Cheers!
Nick

messages.subject_clean: [BioGeoBEARS] Error in if (sum(TF) > 0) { : missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed
messages.body_plain:
It should be fixed now, this is the code that was added today, it checks for negative branchlengths coming from the chainsaw2 function that chops up the tree during time-stratified analyses.  Just now I added "TF[is.na <http://is.na>(TF)] = FALSE" to stop the NA that occurs if e.g. there is no branchlength below the root node.

===================
#######################################################
# Error check
#######################################################
tmp_trtable = prt(tree_to_chainsaw, printflag=FALSE)
brlens = tmp_trtable$edge.length
TF = brlens <= 0
TF[is.na <http://is.na>(TF)] = FALSE
if (sum(TF) > 0)
{
nodenums = (1:nrow(tmp_trtable))[TF]
nodenums
txt = paste0("STOP ERROR in chainsaw2(): the post-chainsaw tree had ", sum(TF), " negative branchlengths. READ THE FOLLOWING ERROR MESSAGE SLOWLY AND CAREFULLY AND YOU MAY FIND A SOLUTION. This error seems to sometimes occur with large cuts on trees with many fossil tips (i.e., non-contemporaneous tips). I'm not sure what causes the bug, except that chainsaw-ing an APE phylo object is quite complex, and it is even more complex for a tree with many non-contemporaneous tips. Imagine a phylogeny made of cardboard, then cutting it at various timepoints, then keeping track of all of the pieces.  Anyway, until I fix it, your best bet is to chainsaw2() in stages, using smaller cuts than the one that caused the error.  Or if you are using BioGeoBEARS and doing a time-stratified analysis, create extra time-strata (perhaps repeating the same settings for several time bins), so that the usage of chainsaw2() within section_the_tree() does not cause an error.")
cat("\n\n")
cat(txt)
cat("\n\n")
stop(txt)
} # END if (sum(TF) > 0)
===================

Cheers, Nick

messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] error in DIVALIKE+J
messages.body_plain:
Hi - hard to say just from this, but usually this kind of thing is underflow errors on Windows machines.  Meaning: the optimizer tries numbers too small and gets negative probabilities or divide-by-0 errors or something.  Usually, the solution is to raise the "min" on d, e, and j so they are slightly further from 0 (search the example script for "min"). E.g.

change
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table["j","min"] = 0.00001
to
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table["j","min"] = 0.001

change
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table["d","min"] = 0.0000001
to
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table["d","min"] = 0.00001

The other option is try a different optimizer, e.g.

Change
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$use_optimx = TRUE
to
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$use_optimx = FALSE

or to

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$use_optimx = "GenSA"

Also, make sure each model has this error trap:
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$on_NaN_error = -1e50

...and that your starting values ("init") are reasonable, i.e. well within the min/max limits.

For "init", "min", etc. see the model table:
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table

Cheers,
Nick

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The NaNs do matter, they probably mean you have set up constraints that make your data impossible (likelihood=0, log-likelihood=-Infinity).

The thing to think about is whether there is a viable series of transitions between your different tips.  E.g. if you had a tip with ABCD but you had excluded ABC, ACD, and BCD from the state space, there would be no way to get to ABCD from any other state.

Main advice: constrain the state space less.

Cheers,
Nick

messages.body_plain:
Hi -- really, you should run all models under the same, good tree.  If you rescaled the tree to make it big enough, there is a chance you will get the same likelihoods and similar parameters between the trees (if you multiplied the branch lengths by 100, the estimates of d and e should come out 100 times lower*).

I have put warnings all over the place on the help pages, but the mistake about using weird, unrealistic trees derived from goodness-knows-where still seems common.

In other words: the tree *must* be something you feel like you can defend in peer-review, or else all the other work you put in is pointless.  I.e., MAKE SURE you have high-quality dating analysis, or a previously published tree, and make sure the tree hasn't been screwed up through some other issue (saving it out from some other program, doing a BEAST analysis without any date calibrations, whatever).  The branch lengths and total tree age should be realistic and defensible.

The fact that your original tree was tiny and you didn't realize it until I pointed it out makes me worry that you are still learning on all of these issues.  Learning is totally fine, of course, but be sure you are clear on this: Before you proceed further with downstream analysis, MAKE SURE you figure out why your original tree was tiny, and make sure that whatever dated tree you decide to use in the end is defensible, then use that good tree for all downstream analyses.**

Cheers,
Nick

* This logic only applies if all parameters are within the min/max bounds for those parameters, under both original and rescaled trees. With the tiny tree you started with this is not guaranteed.

** Or a Bayesian sample of trees or whatever

I would say, if someone just want relative dating in a dated phylogeny, they should just set the root age prior as Normal(mean=10, sd=0.1) or Normal(mean=1, sd=0.001), or something like that.  Then you can just talk about the tree in terms of "relative time units" or something.

This will at least force the tree into a vaguely reasonable parameter space, which can be important as various BEAST priors (for rates etc.) often have defaults that assume something like "the phylogeny will span something between 0.01 and 1000 million years", and other programs make similar assumptions.  The other issue is numeric precision in the computer, if numbers get super-small so that rounding errors etc. start accumulating, all kinds of weird things can happen both in the BEAST analysis and downstream programs (as you observed).

Sorry to jump on the issue, I just see it a lot!

Cheers,
Nick
